newsitem.title: UK: UK welcomes EU plans, wants tougher farm reforms.
newsitem.headline: UK welcomes EU plans, wants tougher farm reforms.

text.p: Britain on Wednesday welcomed proposals to invite six countries to join the European Union but said a related plan to cut farm spending did not go far enough.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said the European Commission's "Agenda 2000" recommendations, which the Brussels-based executive presented earlier to the European Parliament, opened a new chapter in the history of the 15-nation EU.
"I welcome the fact that we are moving away from introspection about our institutions to a new agenda based on the twin aims of enlargement and policy reform," he said in a statement.
"We now have an opportunity both to end the divisions which have scarred our continent since the last war and to shape new policies which will bring real benefits to all our citizens."

Cook supported the Commission's clear recommendation that Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Slovenia and Cyprus be invited into the EU and said he looked forward to negotiations starting in the first half of 1998 during Britain's stint as EU president.
"Enlargement is a central objective for the UK and the EU. We must grasp this historic opportunity to enhance security and prosperity throughout Europe," he said.
Cook said reform of the Common Agricultural Policy, which gobbles up half of the EU budget, was a top priority if enlargement was to be affordable and successful.

Reform also made sound economic sense, but he said the Commission's proposals, which envisage signficant cuts in support prices for beef and cereals compensated by more direct payments to farmers, should only be a first step.
"The Commission's ideas will bring real benefits to consumers, but the UK believes that we will need a still more radical strategy," Cook said.
He welcomed the Commission's proposal that the EU's current spending ceiling, set at 1.27 percent of the bloc's Gross National Product, be maintained through 2006.

Cook accepted that all existing member states would have to accept smaller hand-outs from the EU's structural and cohesion funds, which finance regional, social and agricultural development projects, to free up money for the new entrants.
"But Britain will insist that future arrangements should be fair, and that the necessary reductions take proper account of the UK's regional needs," he added.
